name: Gareth Rahman

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm with the independent Work Futures Panel. We have no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government; this is confidential, and your name won't go in our findings. What does a usual shift involve?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm Gareth, 43, a junior lineworker. At the depot I lay out the grounding clamps and read the job ticket with the crew lead before we take the bucket truck out. I carry the cones and tools, watch how the lead tests the line, and write my questions in a small pocket notebook.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about the work, and what is hard to leave at the depot?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like learning a trade from people who take safety seriously and don't cut corners. The hours can run late, and my partner and I have a mortgage and two children, ages 8 and 17, who depend on my pay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau: Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say a quiet software screen doesn't tell me whether a clamp is seated. If the new form saves the office a minute, fine, but the crew still has to check the equipment before climbing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I don't think a small change takes my field job, since a person still handles the hardware. My wages are low and our savings are thin, so a slow month would make the mortgage hard to manage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep learning the equipment checks from the senior lineworkers and keep my notebook beside the job ticket. I wouldn't change how I verify a pole just because the office prints the order differently.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'm not worried about this small change taking my job, but I am anxious about money already. The mortgage and household bills come before any new purchase.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which equipment check has taken the longest for you to learn?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I had to learn how the grounding clamps fit before we touch the conductor. I ask the lead to watch me do it until he says I can repeat it correctly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do if a new work form and the marked pole number disagreed?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stop and ask the lead to call dispatch for a corrected ticket. I would not decide which number to trust while the crew was already preparing to climb.

say: I say a screen cannot confirm a **grounding clamp** is seated.
I still expect a crew member to check **equipment before climbing**.
think: I don't expect a small software change to take my **field job**.
I worry about the **mortgage** because our savings are thin.
do: Keep learning the **equipment checks** from senior lineworkers.
Use my notebook to record questions about each **job ticket**.
feel: I'm steady about the task but **anxious** about household money.
S0.quote: I'd say a quiet software screen doesn't tell me whether a clamp is seated.
fieldNote: He relies on **hands-on instruction** for equipment checks.
His confidence in the job does not erase **mortgage pressure** from thin savings.
He values **careful repetition** more than a faster form.

steps.text: Keep practising grounding-clamp checks with the senior lineworker

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption: Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd like the order typed cleanly, but I still look at the insulator from the ground. The job lead should be able to correct a route if the paper order doesn't match the site.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I worry that the office could plan more calls with fewer staff and then expect the same crew to cover them faster. I am junior, and a short roster would hit my paycheck before I had enough experience to ask for better work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep taking field shifts and ask the lead to explain any new job ticket before we leave the depot. I would wait to make a career decision until I saw whether our regular maintenance days were actually removed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'm anxious because I don't have another local trade lined up. I prefer a tool once someone has shown it works, but I won't use a screen as a substitute for checking the line.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would count as a real sign that your field work had changed?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If the company stops sending our crew to regular inspections or cancels supervised training, I'd ask the lead what work is being moved. I wouldn't call one rainy week a permanent change.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you decide whether to try a new digital ticket?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd wait until the lead had used it on real jobs and could show the paper version still matches. I don't use AI, and I don't want to be the first person to trust it around a line.

say: I want a clean order, but I still check the **insulator from the ground**.
I expect the lead to correct a **route mismatch** before we go.
think: I worry that **fewer office staff** could mean faster work for the same crew.
I have no **local trade** ready if my roster shrinks.
do: Keep taking **field shifts** and ask the lead about new tickets.
Wait for actual changes to **maintenance days** before choosing a career move.
feel: I'm **anxious** about local hours, and cautious about untested screens.
S1.quote: I'd like the order typed cleanly, but I still look at the insulator from the ground.
fieldNote: He will wait for a **lead's demonstration** before accepting a new digital ticket.
He distinguishes a weather delay from lasting changes to **inspection schedules**.
He wants a **record of reasons** before reacting to a quiet week.

steps.text: Keep taking field shifts while the maintenance roster remains
Wait for confirmed schedule changes before making a career decision

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028: Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the company should give its crews a clear notice period and tell us what training it will pay for. The office work may change in 2028, but the crew still needs someone to test and ground the line.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My hands know the line; my savings do not know how to last three years. I may have field work until robots arrive, but I don't believe the employer must keep my junior place open that long.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Starting now I'd ask the senior crew lead to put my practical training plan in writing and ask when the next paid course runs. In 2028 I would not move into records or scheduling as a safe career, since AGI can do that thinking work. In 2029, if I still have field shifts, I'd take a paid grounding-and-rescue course and keep working while the utility needs crews.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'm anxious because my pay supports the mortgage and the children. A three-year gap before robots gives me some time, but not a guarantee that the company will keep enough work for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your partner at home?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my partner that we should avoid adding a new loan and keep the older car running if it can pass inspection. I would ask my brother to help with after-school pickups if I need to attend a paid course.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make that paid course worth taking?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd need a qualified instructor to supervise the drills and confirm the course counts toward a real field duty. I won't pay from our small reserve for a certificate with no use at work.

say: I want **clear notice** and paid training before crew changes.
I still expect workers to **test and ground** the line.
think: My hands know the line, but my **thin savings** cannot last three years.
I don't expect the employer to protect my junior job until **2031**.
do: Ask for a written **training plan** and the next paid course date.
Take a paid **grounding-and-rescue course** in 2029 if field shifts remain.
Ask my brother for **school pickups** during course days.
feel: I'm **anxious** because the mortgage and children depend on my wages.
S2.quote: My hands know the line; my savings do not know how to last three years.
fieldNote: He is open to practical instruction but not **unfunded certificates**.
He expects **family help** with pickups rather than a loan to attend training.
He rules out scheduling and records after AGI can do **thinking work**.

steps.text: Keep current field shifts while the utility assigns them
Take the paid grounding-and-rescue course in 2029 if offered
Ask a family member for school pickups during course days

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031: Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years gives the company time to train people properly before the planning work disappears. We still need the utility to say how many crews it expects to keep when robots come around 2034.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll be 48 when AGI arrives and 51 when robots arrive. I can get better at linework in five years, but I may still be one of the junior people if crews are cut before the robot date.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I'd keep asking for supervised practice with the insulated pole, or hot stick, and record each task the lead signs off. In 2032, the first year after AGI, I'd keep taking field shifts, take an employer-paid rescue course, and wait for a confirmed roster before looking elsewhere.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'm anxious, but five years is enough to improve if the training happens during paid hours. I can't afford to leave the roster for a course that might not lead to field work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want the crew lead to record about your practice?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd want the task, the date, and the name of the person who watched me do it. If the company changes, I need another foreman to see what I have actually done.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make you look for another utility?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If the company stops assigning me supervised hours or cancels the course, I'd check real postings and pay at the other utilities. I would not move the family for a rumor or assume a vacancy lasts.

say: I say five years gives the utility time for **proper training**.
I want a staffing plan for the **2034 robot date**.
think: I'll be **48** at AGI and **51** when robots arrive.
I may improve, but I could still be a **junior worker** when shifts change.
do: Practise with the **insulated pole** and record signed tasks now.
Keep field shifts and take paid rescue training in **2032**.
Wait for a confirmed roster before checking **other utilities**.
feel: I'm **anxious**, but paid training would give me some control.
S3.quote: I'd say five years gives the company time to train people properly before the planning work disappears.
fieldNote: He wants a **signed practice record** that another foreman can review.
He would check **real postings and pay** before moving the family.
He will not assume a new **qualification** guarantees work after 2034.

steps.text: Keep field shifts while the utility assigns supervised work
Take the employer-paid rescue course in 2032 if offered
Wait for confirmed roster changes before checking other employers

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036: Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say a decade gives workers time to improve their trade, but the utility should publish real staffing plans long before 2039. I would not promise my family that the same field work continues just because I get more experience.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll be 53 when AGI arrives and 56 when the robots arrive. The warning helps me ask for more responsibility, but I won't count on records or scheduling as a fallback after AGI.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Starting now I'd finish each practical sign-off and ask when the next paid course is scheduled. In 2037, if field shifts remain, I'd take the company's hands-on rescue training and wait for the real roster before making a family decision about staying or moving.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A decade helps, but our savings still cover less than a month now. I'm anxious about current bills and the fact that robots could reach the work I have spent years learning.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you need to know before you decided whether to move?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd need the destination's actual shift roster, pay, and course schedule, and I'd talk it through with my partner and children. I won't uproot them for a general claim that another town has more work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would help you decide whether to stay in the trade?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd want a real list of field duties, the hours offered, and which practical qualifications the company will fund. I would compare that with the mortgage before I accept any change.

say: I say workers can use the decade to improve, but need **real staffing plans**.
I won't promise my family that field work lasts through **2039**.
think: I'll be **53** at AGI and **56** at the robot date.
I won't rely on **records or scheduling** as protection after AGI.
do: Finish practical sign-offs and request the next **paid course** now.
Take hands-on rescue training in **2037** if shifts remain.
Wait for a real roster before deciding whether to move the **family**.
feel: I'm **anxious** about current bills and the future of my field skills.
S4.quote: I'd say a decade gives workers time to improve their trade, but the utility should publish real staffing plans long before 2039.
fieldNote: He links extra time to **practical qualifications**, not a guaranteed career.
He would compare real rosters, wages, and **family needs** before moving.
He wants **course dates** early enough to coordinate with household bills.

steps.text: Keep completing practical sign-offs while employed
Take the employer-paid rescue course in 2037 if offered
Wait for a real roster before deciding whether the family should move

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because three years until robots is short when I have little saved. I need paid trade training and a straight answer about hours from the people who assign the truck.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: I want a straight answer about hours from the people who assign the truck. If the hours are going to change, I want to know early enough to keep my family from making plans on guesses.

headlineQuote: I want a straight answer about hours from the people who assign the truck.
portrait: Gareth is a **43-year-old junior** lineworker with a partner, two school-age children and a mortgage.
He trusts **hands-on instruction** and keeps a pocket notebook for questions.
His **thin savings** and few nearby employers make reduced hours a real risk.
He values work and paid trade training, while knowing **robots may reach** field tasks.
biggestWorry: AGI by **2028** worries him most because robots may arrive around 2031 before he has time to build savings.
whatWouldHelp: Paid **trade training** and an early, straight answer about hours would help him plan with his family.
